method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: The dollar sits near its highest since April 2025 because markets expect a Federal Reserve rate rise on December 9. New York Fed President John Williams backed that on Monday, November 23, saying inflation will not reach 2% until 2028, even as bets on a larger half-point rise have faded. October PCE inflation on Wednesday, November 25 is the week's test.

EUR.text: The euro sits just below $1.10, near its lowest since April 2025, because the Federal Reserve looks set to keep raising rates faster than the European Central Bank. ECB rate-setter Gediminas Simkus on Monday, November 23 backed a December 17 rise but saw no rush to move again, and an early survey the same day showed Germany strong but France shrinking.

GBP.text: The pound trades near $1.31, close to a one-month low against a dollar lifted by Fed rate-rise bets. An early survey on Monday, November 23 showed UK services growth slowing to a five-month low with more job cuts, which trims the case for another Bank of England rise in December after strong October shop sales had built it up.

JPY.text: The yen gained on Friday, November 20 as US shares fell hard, and most economists expect a Bank of Japan rate rise to 1.50% on December 18. A big share rebound on Monday, November 23, after Nvidia brought back Jensen Huang as its boss, takes much of that safe-place demand back and keeps the dollar near 159 yen ahead of Tokyo prices on Thursday, November 26.

CHF.text: The Swiss franc sits near a one-month low against a dollar lifted by bets on more Federal Reserve rate rises. Iran's vow on Monday, November 23 to fight the US naval blockade by every means keeps some safe-place demand for the franc, while a strong rebound in US shares the same day takes some away.

CAD.text: The Canadian dollar sits near 69.8 US cents, close to its weakest since April 2025, because markets expect the Federal Reserve to raise rates faster than the Bank of Canada. Oil's slide to its lowest since late summer on Monday, November 23 trims Canada's export income, and Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem speaks on the economy and rates on Tuesday, November 24.

AUD.text: The Australian dollar sits near 66 US cents, close to its lowest since January, after Australia lost jobs for a second month and an early business survey on Monday, November 23 showed activity shrinking at its fastest pace in more than five years. A sharp rebound in US shares the same day, led by Nvidia bringing back Jensen Huang, gives some relief, but October inflation on Wednesday, November 25 decides how likely a Reserve Bank of Australia rise on December 8 is.

NZD.text: The New Zealand dollar fell to about 54.6 US cents around the weekend of November 21-22, its lowest in 17 years, as a slide in US shares sent money out of risk-linked currencies. A strong share rebound on Monday, November 23 eases that pull, but low local rates against rising US rates keep it under pressure.

XAU.text: Gold bounced about 2% back above $3,600 an ounce on Monday, November 23, after its worst week since March took it to $3,503, its lowest since September 2025. A warning from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent against raising US rates too far helped, but an expected Federal Reserve rate rise on December 9 still caps the recovery.

OIL.text: Brent crude settled near $89 a barrel and US crude near $80 on Monday, November 23, the lowest since late summer, after President Donald Trump signaled more time for talks with Iran and signs of a growing supply surplus outweighed weekend attacks in the Gulf. OPEC+ sets its 2027 output on Sunday, November 29.

items.headline: Fed has 'work to do' to lower inflation, Williams says
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: New York Fed President John Williams said on Monday, November 23 that the Federal Reserve still has work to do to bring inflation down, and that it must act over time. He sees inflation near 3.5% this year and not back at the 2% goal until 2028.

beats.was: The Fed raised its main rate in September to a 3.75%-4.00% range, and markets expect another quarter-point rise at its December 8-9 meeting, with more in 2027. Governor Christopher Waller has said a half-point move should also be considered.
beats.happened: In a speech in New York on Monday, November 23, Williams, who also serves as vice chair of the committee that sets US rates, said the risk to stable prices has grown while the risk to jobs has shrunk. He expects growth near 2.75% this year and next, and unemployment to slip to about 4% from 4.1%.
beats.means: One of the Fed's most senior voices backs a December rise and hints that rates may keep going up into 2027, because he sees inflation staying above target for two more years.
beats.fx: Support for higher US rates for longer keeps a floor under the dollar against currencies whose central banks are moving more slowly, such as the euro, the Canadian dollar and the Swiss franc, and weighs on gold.

impact.why: A senior Fed voice backs the December rise most traders already expect, and hints at more.
Higher US rates for longer make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive.

items.watch: October PCE inflation, the Fed's preferred price gauge, on Wednesday, November 25.

items.headline: ECB's Simkus says a December rise may not be enough, but there is no rush to move again
items.story_title: Will the ECB raise rates one last time in December?
items.summary: Gediminas Simkus, Lithuania's central bank head and a European Central Bank rate-setter, said on Monday, November 23 that a quarter-point rise in December may not fully tame inflation, but that a further move soon after is not urgent.

beats.was: The ECB has raised its rates twice this year, with euro zone inflation near 4% against a 2% goal, and a third rise at its December 17 meeting is seen as all but certain. Markets expect one or two more rises in 2027.
beats.happened: Speaking in Vienna on Monday, November 23, Simkus said one more quarter-point step might not be sufficient, pointing to early signs of rising wages and prices feeding each other, coming wage talks and low gas stocks. He added that he sees little pressure to act again quickly after December.
beats.means: A December rise looks locked in, but the ECB is signalling a slower pace after that than markets might hope, so its rates are unlikely to catch up with the Federal Reserve's soon.
beats.fx: Confirmation of a December rise gives the euro a little support, but a slow path afterwards does little to close the gap with higher US rates that has pushed the euro to its lowest since April 2025.

impact.why: A December rise is confirmed, but the hint of a long pause after it limits the lift.

items.watch: The ECB's rate decision on Thursday, December 17.

items.headline: Brent oil drops below $90 for the first time since early September
items.story_title: Oil supply: how much is lost to the war, and how fast it comes back
items.summary: Brent crude fell more than 3% to about $89 a barrel on the afternoon of Monday, November 23, its lowest since early September, as worry about too much oil outweighed weekend attacks in the Gulf. US crude fell to about $80.50.

beats.was: Brent closed at about $92.60 on Friday, November 20, after a third straight weekly fall. The International Energy Agency said on November 13 that world supply would beat demand by about 1.7 million barrels a day this quarter, with Gulf exports recovering despite tanker attacks.
beats.happened: Prices slid through the day on Monday, November 23, breaking below $90 by mid-afternoon in London. Libya's biggest oil pipeline briefly stopped after a group shut a valve, then pumping resumed, and the bank JPMorgan repeated that it sees prices in the upper $70s in the first half of 2027.
beats.means: The market now treats the war with Iran as a smaller threat to supply than the growing surplus, so the price premium from the fighting keeps fading. A fresh, clear cut to Gulf flows would be needed to reverse that.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil weighs on the Canadian dollar and Norway's krone through lower export income, and helps big importers like Japan and the euro zone by easing their fuel bills and price pressure.

impact.why: A break below $90 to a two-and-a-half-month low shows supply worries outweighing the war.
Lower oil prices cut Canada's export income.
Cheaper oil eases Japan's import bill.

items.watch: The OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, November 29, where the big producers set their 2027 output.

items.headline: New Zealand dollar falls to its lowest in 17 years against the US dollar
items.story_title: New Zealand's economy and the RBNZ
items.summary: The New Zealand dollar dropped to about 54.6 US cents around the weekend of November 21-22, its weakest since the 2009 financial crisis, and was still near 54.7 cents on Monday, November 23.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand cut rates hard over the past two years, leaving New Zealand with low rates while the US Federal Reserve is raising its own.
beats.happened: After a heavy fall in US shares on Friday, November 20, the currency sank to its lowest level in 17 years, ten falls in a row against the US dollar. A strategist at the bank BNZ put the latest leg down mainly on nervous markets and worries about the AI share boom.
beats.means: The gap between New Zealand and US rates already pulls money away, and when investors get nervous they sell small, risk-linked currencies like this one first.
beats.fx: The New Zealand dollar stays under pressure for as long as share markets keep falling; the Australian dollar faces the same pull.

impact.why: A 17-year low as nervous markets and low local rates push money out.
The same flight from risk-linked currencies weighs on its neighbour.

items.watch: Whether the bounce in US shares on Monday, November 23 holds; a steady recovery would ease the selling.

items.headline: Chicago Fed gauge of US activity slips just below trend in October
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: The Chicago Fed National Activity Index, a broad monthly gauge of the US economy, fell to -0.06 for October, out on Monday, November 23, from +0.05 in September and well short of the +0.4 forecast.

beats.was: Markets expect the Federal Reserve to raise rates on December 9 because US growth and inflation have stayed strong, which has lifted the dollar near its highest since April 2025.
beats.happened: The index, built from 85 measures of output, jobs, spending and orders, moved from slightly above its long-run trend to slightly below it, missing forecasts.
beats.means: A reading near zero means the economy grew about at its normal pace in October, so it is a small sign of cooling rather than a slowdown. It does little to change the case for a December rate rise.
beats.fx: A mild weight on the dollar, easily outweighed by inflation figures due on Wednesday, November 25.

impact.why: Growth gauge misses forecasts but only dips to about trend.

items.watch: October PCE inflation, the Fed's preferred price measure, on Wednesday, November 25.

items.headline: Asian shares slide again on Monday as worries over AI spending spread
items.story_title: AI stocks and the mood in markets
items.summary: South Korea's Kospi index fell as much as 5.8% on Monday, November 23 and Hong Kong's Hang Seng about 1.9%, while Japan's market was shut for a holiday. US stock futures rose about 2%, hinting at a bounce later.

beats.was: On Friday, November 20 the S&P 500 fell 3.7%, putting it more than 10% below its peak, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq lost 5.3%, wiping out its gains for 2026, on fears that huge spending on artificial intelligence won't pay off.
beats.happened: Chip-heavy Asian markets took the next hit when they opened, with Samsung and other tech makers leading the drop, even though South Korea's chip exports for early November jumped.
beats.means: Investors are still pulling money out of tech shares, but rising US futures show some buyers think the sell-off went too far.
beats.fx: When shares fall this hard, the yen and the Swiss franc tend to gain as safe places, while the Australian and New Zealand dollars, tied to global growth, tend to suffer.

impact.why: Another fall in Asian shares weighs on currencies tied to global growth.
Stock selling tends to lift the yen as a safe place, though Japan's market was shut.
Risk-shy investors tend to avoid the New Zealand dollar.

items.watch: Whether US shares follow their futures higher when New York opens on Monday, November 23.

items.headline: European shares claw back some of last week's heavy loss
items.story_title: AI stocks and the mood in markets
items.summary: Europe's STOXX 600 share index rose about 0.3% early on Monday, November 23, led by chipmakers, after its steepest weekly fall since March 2025.

beats.was: Worries that the rush into artificial intelligence shares had gone too far knocked the STOXX 600 down nearly 6% in the week to Friday, November 20, and pushed the S&P 500 in New York into a correction.
beats.happened: Buyers came back at the European open on Monday, November 23: technology shares rose 1.3%, chip-equipment makers such as ASML gained up to 4%, and mining shares rose with a rebound in gold.
beats.means: A calmer start to the week eases the rush into safe places, though a small bounce after a big fall does not show the selling is over.
beats.fx: Steadier shares take some demand away from the yen and Swiss franc and help currencies tied to growth such as the Australian dollar.

impact.why: Calmer shares cut demand for the yen as a safe place.
Better mood helps a currency tied to global growth.
Less need for a safe place.

items.watch: Whether the bounce holds through the US open on Monday, November 23, after the S&P 500 fell 3.7% on Friday, November 20.

items.headline: Euro zone business growth holds up as Germany speeds ahead and France sinks
items.story_title: Will the ECB raise rates one last time in December?
items.summary: S&P Global's early November business survey for the euro zone, out on Monday, November 23, held at 51.7, a little short of forecasts, with Germany at a four-year high and France shrinking faster.

beats.was: The European Central Bank is expected to raise rates again in December, but the euro has slid below $1.10 because the US Federal Reserve looks set to raise faster.
beats.happened: The survey of purchasing managers stayed at 51.7 (above 50 means growth) against 51.9 forecast: factories did better than expected while services slipped to a five-month low. Germany hit its best reading since March 2022, while France fell to a six-month low as next year's presidential election weighs on firms.
beats.means: Overall growth is steady, which keeps a December ECB rate rise on the table, but softer services, falling business confidence and easing cost pressure give no reason to raise faster.
beats.fx: A mixed result gives the euro little lift against a dollar backed by expected Fed rate rises.

impact.why: Steady growth but a small miss, with Germany strong and France weak.

items.watch: Euro zone inflation figures for November, due in early December, the last big reading before the ECB's December decision.

items.headline: Oil Falls as Trump Signals Iran Talks
items.story_title: Oil supply: how much is lost to the war, and how fast it comes back
items.summary: US crude fell 4.5% to settle near $80.17 a barrel on Monday, November 23, its lowest close since August, and Brent settled 3.5% lower at about $89.37, after President Donald Trump signaled he would give talks with Iran more time.

beats.was: Brent has lost about a fifth of its value in November as Gulf exports recover despite tanker attacks, and the International Energy Agency expects world supply to beat demand by about 2 million barrels a day this quarter.
beats.happened: Trump told Fox News he would allow more time for diplomacy with Iran and might resume the war next year if talks fail, while warning ships that test the US blockade. Prices fell through the day even after Iran attacked Bahrain over the weekend of November 21-22.
beats.means: With the US leaning toward talks and oil still flowing out of the Gulf, the market keeps shrinking the price premium it had added for the war. Only a clear new cut to supply looks likely to turn prices back up.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil cuts export income for Canada and Norway and eases fuel bills and price pressure for big importers like Japan, the euro zone and India.

impact.why: A move toward talks plus a growing surplus pushed US crude to its lowest close since August.
Lower oil prices cut Canada's export income.
Cheaper oil eases Japan's import bill.

items.watch: The OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, November 29, where the big producers set their 2027 output.

items.headline: Oil slips as more supply outweighs Gulf attacks, and JPMorgan sees the upper $70s next year
items.story_title: Oil supply: how much is lost to the war, and how fast it comes back
items.summary: Brent crude fell about $1.30 to near $91.25 a barrel by mid-morning in Europe on Monday, November 23, as signs of more oil coming to market outweighed weekend attacks in the Gulf. The bank JPMorgan expects Brent to fall into the upper $70s in the first half of 2027.

beats.was: Oil has stayed high through the US-Israeli war with Iran, with ships attacked near the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carries about a fifth of the world's oil. Brent still fell about 4% in the week to Friday, November 20.
beats.happened: Yemen's Houthi group said it hit a Saudi oil refinery on Sunday, November 22, and ships were attacked near Hormuz, yet prices fell. Libya reopened the pipeline from Sharara, its biggest oil field, and JPMorgan pointed to rising output in the Middle East and the Americas, led by the US.
beats.means: Traders are giving more weight to extra supply than to the attacks, so the war's price premium keeps shrinking unless the fighting clearly cuts flows. OPEC+, the group of big producers led by Saudi Arabia and Russia, sets its 2027 output on Sunday, November 29.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil trims income for oil exporters like Canada and Norway and eases import bills and price pressure for big buyers such as Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: More supply and a bank forecast of lower prices outweigh the attacks for now.
Lower oil prices mean less export income for Canada.
Cheaper oil eases Japan's import bill.

items.watch: The OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, November 29; a plan to pump more in 2027 would add to the pressure on prices.

items.headline: US shares leap as Nvidia brings back Jensen Huang as its boss
items.story_title: AI stocks and the mood in markets
items.summary: Nvidia's board put co-founder Jensen Huang back in charge on Monday, November 23, and US share prices jumped about 4% for the S&P 500 and about 6% for the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 before the open, after their worst week since 2020.

beats.was: Jensen Huang quit as Nvidia's chief executive on November 12 amid a board review of his business ties, and the chipmaker's fall helped drag the S&P 500 down more than 10% from its October record by Friday, November 20.
beats.happened: The board named Huang president, chief executive and board chair again, effective at once, though its review goes on. Nvidia rose about 27% before the open, and other chip makers such as AMD, Broadcom and Micron rose 4-5%.
beats.means: The biggest single worry behind last week's share slide has eased, so investors are less eager to hide in safe places and more willing to own riskier assets again.
beats.fx: A calmer mood tends to lift risk-linked currencies like the Australian and New Zealand dollars and take some safe-place demand away from the yen and the Swiss franc.

impact.why: A sharp bounce in shares pulls money back into risk-linked currencies.
Less need for a safe place to park money as shares recover.
Eases the risk selling that took it to a 17-year low.
Safe-place demand fades as markets calm.

items.watch: Whether shares hold the gains into October PCE inflation on Wednesday, November 25; a quick fade would bring last week's nerves back.

items.headline: Iran says safe shipping through Hormuz can return quickly if the US meets its terms
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday, November 23 that security in the Strait of Hormuz could be restored very quickly if the US keeps its commitments and accepts Iran's conditions. He called those conditions Iran's rights, not new demands.

beats.was: Ships near the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carries about a fifth of the world's oil, have been attacked through the US-Israeli war with Iran, and the US Navy is blockading Iranian shipping. Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi had said the strait could reopen within two hours on the right terms.
beats.happened: At his weekly briefing in Tehran, Baghaei backed that line and said Iran's terms are not fresh preconditions. He also said no decision to leave the global nuclear arms treaty has reached the Foreign Ministry.
beats.means: Iran keeps a door open to a deal that would calm shipping, but only on its own terms, and there is no sign yet that the US has agreed. Talk alone does not change oil flows.
beats.fx: Any real step toward reopening Hormuz would lower oil and cut demand for safe places like the Swiss franc and gold. Until then the effect is small.

impact.why: Iran signals shipping could return to normal fast, but only if the US accepts its terms.
Talk of calmer shipping trims safe-place demand, but nothing is agreed.

items.watch: Whether the US answers Iran's terms; a reply would matter far more than statements from either side.

items.headline: Oil slides despite weekend attacks as shipping costs and cargo premiums cool
items.story_title: Oil supply: how much is lost to the war, and how fast it comes back
items.summary: Brent crude fell about 1.8% to near $90.90 a barrel on Monday, November 23, even after weekend attacks on ships and Gulf sites, as the extra cost of shipping and buying physical oil keeps fading.

beats.was: The war with Iran and attacks near the Strait of Hormuz pushed oil sharply higher in October, but prices have fallen for three weeks as Gulf exports held up.
beats.happened: Over the weekend of November 21-22, ships near Hormuz were hit, Bahrain said an Iranian attack struck an industrial site, and Yemen's Houthis claimed an unconfirmed strike on a Saudi refinery. Prices fell anyway. Goldman Sachs said Atlantic crude shipping costs are 60-70% below their October peak, and cargoes now sell about $1 above futures prices, against about $31 in early October.
beats.means: Buyers are getting the oil they need, so the market no longer pays much extra for fear of lost supply. Attacks now need to actually cut flows to lift prices.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil trims export income for Canada and eases price pressure for big importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Fading supply premium outweighs weekend attacks.
Lower crude trims Canada's export income.

items.watch: OPEC+ setting 2027 output on Sunday, November 29, and any attack that actually halts Gulf exports.

items.headline: Iran vows to use every means against the US naval blockade
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's foreign ministry said on Monday, November 23 it will use every means to break the US naval blockade of its ports, a day after President Trump warned Iranian ships off.

beats.was: The US Navy is blockading Iran's ports as part of the war, and on Sunday, November 22 President Donald Trump said Iranian ships trying to break it would be sunk.
beats.happened: At his weekly briefing on Monday, November 23, Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei called the blockade a crime and promised to fight it by every means, while Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the Strait of Hormuz could reopen quickly if the US lifts sanctions and the blockade.
beats.means: Both sides are hardening their words but no convoy plan has been announced, and Iran is still naming terms for a deal, so this raises the risk of a clash at sea more than it changes oil flows now.
beats.fx: Sharper threats keep a war risk in the oil price and give some support to safe places such as the Swiss franc and gold.

impact.why: Higher risk of a naval clash near Hormuz, though no supply lost yet.
Tougher war talk adds a little safe-place demand.

items.watch: Whether Iran sends ships to test the blockade, and talks between Qatar's prime minister and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

items.headline: UK services growth slows to a five-month low in early November survey
items.story_title: Bank of England: how far do rates rise?
items.summary: S&P Global's early November survey of UK purchasing managers, out on Monday, November 23, showed services growth slowing to a five-month low, well short of forecasts.

beats.was: The Bank of England has been raising rates to cool inflation, and strong October shop sales had firmed bets on another rise in December.
beats.happened: The services reading fell to 52.0 from 52.8, against 53.0 forecast, and the factory reading slipped to 52.7. Export orders for services fell the most since early 2021 and firms cut staff again, while factory output rose at its fastest pace in more than two years.
beats.means: Growth is still positive but cooling, and slower price rises charged by firms point to easing inflation pressure, which makes it a little harder for the Bank of England to justify more rate rises.
beats.fx: A clear miss in the larger services side weighs on the pound, which slipped back from its early high against the dollar.

impact.why: Services miss by a full point and job cuts trim the case for more BoE rises.

items.watch: Comments from Bank of England Chief Economist Huw Pill, due to speak on Monday, November 23, for any hint on a December rate rise.

items.headline: Oil stays in a narrow band as weekend Gulf attacks are weighed against ample supply
items.story_title: Oil supply: Gulf flows vs war risk
items.summary: Brent crude eased about 0.5% to near $92.10 a barrel on Monday, November 23, staying in a tight range after weekend attacks around the Gulf.

beats.was: Brent lost about 4% last week, its third weekly fall, because Gulf oil is still flowing and a supply surplus is expected next year despite the war with Iran.
beats.happened: Over the weekend the Houthis of Yemen claimed a strike on a Saudi oil refinery, Bahrain said Iran hit a civilian industrial site, and UK maritime officials reported more attacks on ships near Hormuz, yet Brent moved less than a dollar on Monday, November 23.
beats.means: Traders are treating the attacks as a steady background risk rather than a sign that supply will be lost, and one analyst expects prices to stay in a range to year-end.
beats.fx: A flat oil price gives little new push to oil-linked currencies such as the Canadian dollar and Norwegian krone, or to fuel importers such as Japan.

impact.why: Attack risk offset by strong Gulf flows and a supply surplus.
Oil holds near $92, no fresh lift or drag for Canada's exports.

items.watch: The OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, November 29, which sets the group's output for 2027.

items.headline: Iranian lawmaker claims Iran hits about 10 tankers a day near Hormuz
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: An Iranian member of parliament said on Monday, November 23 that Iran strikes around 10 tankers a day that break its rules in the Strait of Hormuz, a claim far above the attacks confirmed by shipping monitors.

beats.was: Since the war began in late February, Iran has limited traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about a fifth of the world's oil before the conflict, and the US Navy blockades Iran's ports.
beats.happened: Iranian lawmaker Abolfazl Aboutorabi said on Monday, November 23 that Iran hits about 10 tankers a day and that the strait will not go back to how it was before the war. The UK's maritime security agency, UKMTO, confirmed 39 incidents in all of October, its highest monthly count of the war.
beats.means: The claim is not backed by the confirmed counts, which are far lower, so it reads more as a warning to shippers than proof of a new wave of attacks. Confirmed attacks are still rising month by month, though.
beats.fx: Talk like this keeps a war risk in the oil price, but oil has been falling because Gulf exports are still flowing well, so the push is small.

impact.why: An unconfirmed claim of daily tanker attacks adds to supply worries, without any confirmed loss of oil.

items.watch: Whether UKMTO's November count of confirmed attacks tops October's 39.

items.headline: Gold bounces back above $3,600 an ounce in early Monday trade
items.story_title: Gold vs Fed rate rises
items.summary: Spot gold rose about 2% to above $3,600 an ounce in Asian trading on Monday, November 23, and silver gained about 3%, after both had their worst week in months.

beats.was: Gold fell to about $3,503 on Friday, November 20, its lowest since September 2025, as investors sold it along with shares and bet on more Federal Reserve rate rises.
beats.happened: Buyers came back as the week opened, helped by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warning on Sunday, November 22 that the Fed could raise rates too far, and by a slightly softer dollar.
beats.means: Talk of a smaller or slower set of Fed rate rises takes some pressure off gold, which pays no interest and suffers when US rates climb.
beats.fx: A firmer gold price reflects a small step back from the dollar, but markets still expect a quarter-point Fed rise on December 9.

impact.why: A 2% rebound after a heavy weekly loss, helped by softer talk on Fed rate rises.
Bessent's warning trims bets on bigger Fed rate rises.

items.watch: US October PCE inflation on Wednesday, November 25, the Federal Reserve's preferred price measure, ahead of its December 9 decision.

items.headline: Oil slips at the start of the week as strong Gulf exports and a supply surplus outweigh Iran's attacks
items.story_title: Oil supply: how much is lost to the war, and how fast it comes back
items.summary: Brent crude fell 0.8% to about $91.85 a barrel as trading reopened late on Sunday, November 22, even after a weekend of Iranian and Houthi attacks around the Gulf, including a Houthi claim of a strike on Saudi Arabia's Rabigh refinery.

beats.was: Brent is down about 20% in November after President Trump held off new strikes on Iran following the US midterm elections, and Gulf exports have stayed close to pre-war levels.
beats.happened: Oil fell despite Trump saying he leans toward new strikes on Iran after the New Year if talks fail, fresh Iranian attacks on Bahrain, and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
beats.means: Traders are giving more weight to a coming supply surplus, about 2 million barrels a day in the last quarter according to the International Energy Agency, than to the war's threats so far.
beats.fx: Softer oil trims export income for Canada and Norway and eases fuel costs for importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Strong Gulf exports and a forecast surplus outweigh the weekend's attacks.
Lower oil prices cut Canada's export income.

items.watch: The OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, November 29 on output, and whether ship crossings through Hormuz keep falling.

items.headline: Australian business activity shrinks at its fastest pace in more than five years
items.story_title: Will the RBA raise rates again in December?
items.summary: S&P Global's early survey of Australian purchasing managers for November, out on Monday, November 23 (local time), fell to 46.1 from 48.2, with services at 46.2 and factories at 48.7. Any reading under 50 means activity is shrinking.

beats.was: Australia had already lost jobs for two months in a row, and the Reserve Bank of Australia was split at its November meeting on whether to keep raising rates.
beats.happened: Firms reported falling output, the first drop in new orders in five months, more job cuts and their weakest outlook in three years, while their costs and selling prices rose more slowly.
beats.means: A shrinking economy with cooling price pressure gives the Reserve Bank of Australia more reason to stop raising rates at its December 8 meeting.
beats.fx: Fewer expected rate rises in Australia, while the Federal Reserve keeps signalling more, weigh on the Australian dollar.

impact.why: A deeper slump in business activity lowers the odds of another Australian rate rise.

items.watch: Australia's October inflation figure on Wednesday, November 25, the last big reading before the Reserve Bank of Australia meets on December 8.

items.headline: The dollar eases slightly from its highest in 19 months as Asian trading starts
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: The dollar slipped a touch from its highest since April 2025 as trading began in Asia on Monday, November 23. Futures still put about an 89% chance on a quarter-point Federal Reserve rate rise on December 9, but bets on a larger half-point rise have gone.

beats.was: The dollar climbed to its highest in about a year and a half last week as markets came to expect another Federal Reserve rate rise in December and US stocks fell sharply.
beats.happened: The euro edged up to about $1.097, the Australian dollar to about 66.3 US cents, and the dollar rose slightly to about 158.6 yen, with Japan's markets shut for a holiday.
beats.means: Markets still expect one more Fed rise in December, but no longer a bigger one, after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned against raising rates too far.
beats.fx: Smaller rate-rise bets take a little steam out of the dollar, though it stays near its highs.

impact.why: Bets on a larger Fed rate rise in December have faded, a small loss of support for the dollar.
The euro edges up as the dollar eases slightly.

items.watch: US October PCE inflation, the Fed's preferred price gauge, on Wednesday, November 25, ahead of the Fed meeting of December 8 to 9.

items.headline: New Zealand shop sales jump 2.2% in the third quarter
items.story_title: New Zealand's economy and the RBNZ
items.summary: Statistics New Zealand said on Monday, November 23 (local time) that the volume of retail sales rose 2.2% in July to September, more than four times the 0.5% economists expected, after a fall in April to June.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand has held its rate at 2.75% while the New Zealand dollar sits near its lowest since the pandemic, and spending had shrunk in the second quarter.
beats.happened: Shoppers bought clearly more in the third quarter, and the value of sales rose in every region of the country.
beats.means: New Zealand households are spending more than expected, which makes further rate cuts from the Reserve Bank less likely.
beats.fx: A firmer economy gives the New Zealand dollar some support against a strong US dollar.

impact.why: A large beat on spending lowers the odds of more rate cuts in New Zealand.

items.watch: Whether the New Zealand dollar holds its gain as Asian markets open, with Japan closed for a holiday on Monday, November 23.

items.headline: China, South Korea and Taiwan move to calm stock markets after the US slide
items.story_title: AI stocks and the mood in markets
items.summary: Ahead of Monday, November 23, China eased margin rules for stock buyers, South Korea readied its market stabilisation fund for the first time since 2008, and Taiwan widened limits on short selling after its worst week in 35 years.

beats.was: The S&P 500 fell into a correction last week and the Nasdaq 100 had its worst week since March 2020, as worries about artificial-intelligence spending spread to Asian chip stocks.
beats.happened: Asian governments stepped in with measures to support their stock markets, while Asian shares stood about 18% below their June peak, near a bear market. Japan's markets are closed on Monday, November 23 for a holiday.
beats.means: Officials are worried enough to act, but the fear in markets has not yet eased, and Asian trading may stay rough.
beats.fx: Continued stock market fear tends to help the yen and Swiss franc and hurt currencies tied to global growth, such as the Australian dollar.

impact.why: Weak Asian stock markets weigh on a currency tied to regional growth.
Stock market fear adds some demand for the yen as a safe place.

items.watch: Whether the support steps steady Asian shares through Monday, November 23, and how US stocks open after last week's slide.

items.headline: Bessent warns the Fed against raising rates too far
items.story_title: The Federal Reserve's rate rises
items.summary: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on CBS's Face the Nation on Sunday, November 22 that the Federal Reserve could make a policy mistake if it raises rates too much, after US stocks fell into a correction.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve raised its rate to 3.75%-4.00% in September, and markets now almost fully expect another quarter-point rise on December 9.
beats.happened: Bessent pointed to tough talk from Fed governors and a sharp tightening in borrowing conditions as stocks slid. He has made similar points in TV interviews on November 13 and 20.
beats.means: The government is pushing back against more Fed rate rises, but the Fed sets rates on its own and this does not change its plan by itself.
beats.fx: Adds a little doubt to the case for bigger Fed rises, which takes some shine off the dollar.

impact.why: Treasury pressure against more rate rises slightly lowers the odds of a bigger Fed move, though a December rise is still expected.

items.watch: Whether Fed officials answer Bessent before Thanksgiving on Thursday, November 26, and October's PCE inflation on Wednesday, November 25.

items.headline: Trump says he leans toward new strikes on Iran after New Year if talks fail
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: US President Donald Trump told Fox News on Sunday, November 22 that he is inclined to restart strikes on Iran after the New Year if indirect talks bring no deal, and that Iranian ships trying to break the US naval blockade would be sunk.

beats.was: The US and Israel went to war with Iran in February, a framework deal was signed in June, and fighting has flared on and off since July while the US Navy blocks Iran's ports.
beats.happened: Trump dismissed Iran's negotiators as stalling and said US forces would fire on any vessel that tries to cross the blockade. Qatar is passing messages between the two sides.
beats.means: Talks look shakier, and the risk of a bigger war in early 2027 has gone up, though nothing has changed on the water yet.
beats.fx: Keeps a risk premium in oil and some demand for safe currencies as markets reopen.

impact.why: A threat of renewed US strikes raises the chance of more lost Gulf supply, but it is a warning, not an action.
More war risk adds some demand for the franc as a safe place.

items.watch: Whether an Iranian tanker tries to cross the blockade, and any sign of progress or collapse in the Qatar-relayed talks.

items.headline: Iran says two supertankers hit sea mines near Hormuz
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's navy said on Sunday, November 22 that two supertankers struck sea mines and stopped after sailing into a zone it bars near the Strait of Hormuz. The UK's maritime security agency separately reported a tanker in an incident with military forces in the Gulf of Oman, off Chabahar in Iran.

beats.was: The US-Iran war began in late February, and the US Navy has blocked Iran's oil exports for months while Iran has stepped up attacks on other countries' tankers.
beats.happened: Iranian media quoting the Revolutionary Guards navy said two very large tankers caught fire after hitting mines north of Ghanam Island and east of the strait. The ships were not named and the claim has not been confirmed. The UK agency's report came the same day as word that an Iranian tanker may have left Kharg Island to try to slip past the US blockade.
beats.means: If mines are now in the sea lanes, crossing Hormuz gets much riskier for every tanker, not just those Iran picks out.
beats.fx: Adds to the risk of lost Gulf oil just before markets reopen, which supports oil and safe currencies.

impact.why: Mines near the strait would threaten a route that carries a large share of the world's oil, though Iran's claim is not yet confirmed.
A new kind of threat to shipping adds some demand for the franc as a safe place.
Higher oil prices lift Canada's export income.

items.watch: Whether shipping firms or the US Navy confirm the mine strikes and name the ships, and how oil trades once markets reopen on the evening of Sunday, November 22.

items.headline: Attacks on ships around Hormuz are running at the war's highest pace
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: A CNN count of UK maritime reports, published on Sunday, November 22, finds at least 22 attacks on ships near Hormuz so far in November, after more than 30 in October, against about 10 a month earlier in the war. Ship-tracker Kpler says Iranian oil afloat outside the US blockade has fallen to zero.

beats.was: The US-Iran war began in late February, and the US Navy has blocked Iran's oil exports for months while Gulf exports from other countries recovered and oil prices fell.
beats.happened: Reported attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf and the Gulf of Oman jumped in October and stayed high in November. Three tankers leaving the strait were hit on Friday, November 20 and Saturday, November 21, which a risk firm called likely Iranian work.
beats.means: Iran is losing its oil income to the blockade and is pushing back by making the sea route riskier for everyone else.
beats.fx: Keeps a war-risk floor under oil even as Gulf exports recover, and adds some steady demand for safe currencies.

impact.why: More attacks on tankers raise the risk of lost Gulf barrels, though exports have kept flowing so far.
A rising pace of attacks keeps some safe-haven demand for the franc.

items.watch: Whether November's attack count passes October's, and whether insurers or shippers start avoiding the strait again.

items.headline: Iran's Guards say they hit US air-defence radars in Bahrain
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Sunday, November 22 that missiles and drones destroyed two US Patriot air-defence radars at bases in Bahrain, home of the US Navy's Fifth Fleet. The claim has not been confirmed.

beats.was: Bahrain said an Iranian strike on Saturday, November 21 set fire to a civilian industrial site, one of several Iranian attacks around the Gulf in the past week.
beats.happened: The Guards called the radar strikes payback for a US strike on an Iranian radar on Hengam Island. UK maritime data showed ship crossings of Hormuz fell 15% in the week to November 18, with oil tankers down to 37 from 52.
beats.means: Iran is now aiming directly at US forces in a Gulf state, which widens the war beyond attacks on ships.
beats.fx: Raises the chance of a larger US-Iran clash, a mild push for oil and safe currencies.

impact.why: Strikes on US bases in the Gulf raise the risk of a wider war near oil routes, though the damage is unconfirmed.
Direct attacks on US forces add some safe-haven demand.

items.watch: Whether the US confirms damage in Bahrain or answers with new strikes on Iran.

items.headline: Fewer ships cross Hormuz as Iran steps up attacks
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: About 25 tankers have been hit near Hormuz in the week to Sunday, November 22, Al Jazeera reports, and ships crossing the strait fell 15% in the week of November 12-18, with oil tankers down from 52 to 37. Iran also said it shot down another US drone that same day.

beats.was: Since the war began in late February, the US Navy has blocked Iran's oil exports, and traffic through the strait had been recovering toward pre-war levels.
beats.happened: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they hit US radar sites in Bahrain on Saturday, November 21 and downed a fourth US drone in 24 hours on Sunday, November 22. UK maritime data show 263 ships crossed the strait in the week of November 12-18, well below the roughly 135 a day before the war.
beats.means: The rise in attacks is starting to show up in traffic, the first sign in weeks that Gulf oil flows could shrink again.
beats.fx: Backs oil and the currencies that gain from it, like the Canadian dollar, and hurts big oil buyers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Tanker crossings fell by about a quarter in one week, a real hit to the supply that had been coming back.
Japan imports almost all its oil, so a pricier, scarcer supply weighs on the yen.
Canada exports oil, so tighter Gulf supply helps its income.

items.watch: Next week's UK maritime count of crossings, to see whether traffic falls further.

items.headline: Saudi air defences destroy a Houthi drone flying toward Riyadh on Sunday, November 22
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Saudi air defences shot down a Houthi drone headed for Riyadh on Sunday, November 22, hours after stopping a missile aimed at the kingdom's Red Sea coast. No damage or injuries were reported.

beats.was: Yemen's Houthi group, which is backed by Iran, has been firing missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia during the Iran war, and one hit the Saudi wealth fund's tower in Riyadh on Thursday, November 19.
beats.happened: Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said air defences destroyed a Houthi drone flying toward Riyadh. Earlier the same day the coalition stopped a ballistic missile aimed at the west coast, home to the Yanbu oil export terminal and the Jazan refinery.
beats.means: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia now come almost daily, so the threat to Saudi oil sites stays real even though these strikes caused no harm.
beats.fx: Adds a little to the war risk in oil before markets reopen, with no supply lost.

impact.why: Houthi fire near Saudi oil sites keeps supply risk alive, though nothing was hit.
More Gulf attacks add a little demand for the franc as a safe place.

items.watch: Whether a Houthi strike damages a Saudi oil terminal or refinery, which would hit supply rather than just raise the risk.

items.headline: An Iranian tanker said to be running the US blockade turns out to be a fake signal
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Ship-tracking data seemed to show an Iranian tanker sailing through the Strait of Hormuz past the US blockade, but the monitoring group TankerTrackers said on Sunday, November 22 that the ship does not exist. More than 14 tankers still wait at Iran's Kharg Island oil terminal.

beats.was: The US Navy has blocked Iran's oil exports for 130 days in a row, and Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said on Friday, November 20 that the blockade must be broken.
beats.happened: Public ship-tracking signals showed a tanker named Khat-Shekan moving through the strait. TankerTrackers called it a spoof, saying satellite pictures showed no such ship.
beats.means: Iran has not yet broken the blockade, so its oil stays bottled up at Kharg Island and the tanker convoy there is still only a threat.
beats.fx: Takes a little heat out of fears of a sea clash before markets reopen, but leaves Iran's oil off the market.

impact.why: No blockade run means no clash yet, but Iranian barrels stay off the market.

items.watch: Whether the tankers gathered at Kharg Island actually sail, which would test the US Navy directly.

items.headline: Iran says it alone controls Hormuz as a Houthi missile is shot down over western Saudi Arabia
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: On Sunday, November 22 Iran's army said Tehran, not foreign navies, controls the Strait of Hormuz and called that a block to peace talks. Saudi-led forces said they shot down a Houthi missile fired at western Saudi Arabia.

beats.was: The US and Israel went to war with Iran in late February. The US now blockades Iranian ports and escorts ships through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carries about a fifth of the world's oil, while Iran says ships must ask its permission to pass.
beats.happened: A day after Iran's attack on Bahrain, Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said Iran controls the strait and that this stands in the way of talks to end the war. Separately, the Saudi-led coalition said it stopped a ballistic missile from Yemen's Houthi group aimed at the kingdom's west, and a brief danger alert for Mecca province was lifted. Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said no change has been made to Iran's ban on nuclear weapons, though he admitted some at home argue for one.
beats.means: Neither side is offering a path to a ceasefire, so the risk to Gulf shipping stays in place going into the new week. The words add little new on their own, since nothing was hit and no oil route was closed.
beats.fx: Keeps a small war premium in oil and a little support for safe currencies when markets reopen.

impact.why: Iran's claim over Hormuz and more Houthi fire keep the risk to Gulf supply alive, though no supply was lost.
No sign of peace talks keeps some demand for the franc as a safe place.

items.watch: Whether Iran tries to stop escorted ships in the strait, and how oil trades when markets reopen on the evening of Sunday, November 22.

items.headline: Oil heads into a quiet holiday week with an OPEC+ output meeting set for Sunday, November 29
items.story_title: Oil supply: Gulf flows vs war risk
items.summary: Brent ended Friday, November 20 at $92.57 a barrel after a third weekly fall. The next big date for oil is the OPEC+ ministers' meeting on Sunday, November 29, which sets output plans for 2027.

beats.was: Oil prices jumped when the war with Iran began in late February, but they have fallen for three weeks in a row because tankers are again moving close to pre-war amounts out of the Gulf.
beats.happened: Brent rose 0.6% on Friday, November 20 but still lost about 3.4% on the week. OPEC+, the group of big oil producers led by Saudi Arabia and Russia, meets on Sunday, November 29 to set 2027 output using a fresh review of how much each member can pump. The January Brent contract also expires on Monday, November 30, and the next one trades about $2.60 lower.
beats.means: With US markets closed on Thursday, November 26 for Thanksgiving, trading may be thin, so attacks on ships can move prices more than usual. Until the OPEC+ meeting, supply news from the Gulf is the main driver.
beats.fx: Mixed for oil. The oil price feeds straight into the Canadian dollar, and cheaper oil eases inflation worries in Japan and Europe.

impact.why: A preview: OPEC+ could add or hold supply, while Gulf attacks keep some risk in the price.
Canada's export income follows the oil price, which has no clear push until the OPEC+ meeting.

items.watch: What OPEC+ decides on Sunday, November 29, and whether the attacks on tankers near Hormuz slow Gulf exports again.

items.headline: Iranian attack sets an industrial site in Bahrain on fire as Iran says it aimed at US bases
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Bahrain said an Iranian attack late on Saturday, November 21 hit a civilian industrial site and started a fire, with damage but no injuries. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they fired missiles and drones at US military bases in Bahrain.

beats.was: Bahrain, a small Gulf island state, hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet and has been a target since the US and Israel went to war with Iran in late February. After weeks of calm, it faced three drone attacks in the days before Saturday, November 21.
beats.happened: Bahrain's military said its air defences stopped several Iranian attacks late on Saturday, November 21, but one hit a civilian industrial site, which caught fire. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they targeted US positions at the al-Riffa and Awali bases and destroyed two Patriot air-defence radars, a claim not confirmed by the US. Iran called it a reply to US drone flights over its land.
beats.means: Iran is widening its attacks from ships near Hormuz to a Gulf state that hosts US forces, which raises the chance of a US strike back. Markets were shut for the weekend, so the first reaction comes when trading reopens on the evening of Sunday, November 22.
beats.fx: Adds war risk to oil and a little demand for safe currencies such as the yen and Swiss franc.

impact.why: An attack on Gulf soil, not just ships, raises the risk that the war hits oil supply again.
Worries about a wider war add demand for the franc as a safe place.
Some investors buy the yen when war risk rises.

items.watch: Whether the US answers the attack on its bases in Bahrain, and how oil opens on the evening of Sunday, November 22.

items.headline: Two more tankers are hit in the Strait of Hormuz as Iran tightens its hold on shipping
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Two tankers were struck by unknown projectiles off Oman's Khasab coast on Saturday, November 21, with no one hurt. Iran said a separate tanker hit a sea mine east of the strait after ignoring its warnings.

beats.was: The Strait of Hormuz, the sea lane between Iran and Oman that carried about a fifth of the world's oil before the war, has seen ships hit almost daily in November. Iran wants ships to follow lanes it sets, and the US has answered by blockading Iran's ports and escorting tankers.
beats.happened: The UK Maritime Trade Operations, a British navy office that tracks shipping risks, reported one tanker hit at the rear about 20 km north of Khasab and another hit in the engine room about 31 km east, within an hour. Iran's navy said a tanker that had switched off its tracking gear hit a mine and caught fire, which could not be checked independently.
beats.means: Iran's own military counts about 25 tanker incidents in the week to Saturday, November 21. So far oil keeps flowing near pre-war levels, which is why prices fell for three weeks, but each hit raises shipping and insurance costs.
beats.fx: A small lift for oil against its recent slide, and a little support for safe currencies.

impact.why: More ships hit near Hormuz, though exports have kept flowing so far.
Ongoing attacks keep some demand for the franc as a safe place.

items.watch: Whether any ship owners stop sending tankers through Hormuz, and whether the US changes how it escorts them.

items.headline: A short US week puts the Fed's preferred inflation gauge up on Wednesday, November 25
items.story_title: Fed rate rises
items.summary: The Thanksgiving week packs most US data into Wednesday, November 25, led by October's PCE inflation, the measure the Federal Reserve targets. Futures show a near-certain quarter-point Fed rate rise on Wednesday, December 9.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve has been raising rates to fight inflation pushed up by the oil shock from the Iran war, and its October meeting minutes showed nearly all officials expect more rises. That has lifted the dollar to its highest since April 2025.
beats.happened: Monday, November 23 brings early business surveys (PMIs) for Germany, the euro area, the UK and the US. Wednesday, November 25 brings October PCE inflation, expected to show prices excluding food and energy up 0.3% on the month with the yearly rate rising to about 3.2%, plus revised third-quarter growth, durable goods orders, the Fed's Beige Book and Australia's October inflation. US markets close on Thursday, November 26 and shut early on Friday, November 27.
beats.means: A PCE reading at or above forecast would back the December rate rise markets already expect. A softer one could trim talk of a bigger move or of further rises in 2027.
beats.fx: A firm PCE reading would support the dollar, while a soft one would ease some of its lift.

impact.why: A preview: the PCE reading could confirm or soften the expected December Fed rise.
Australia's October inflation on Wednesday, November 25 shapes the Reserve Bank of Australia's next move.

items.watch: October core PCE on Wednesday, November 25: above 0.3% on the month would firm bets on Fed rises beyond December.

items.headline: Iran's foreign minister says talks with the US are still open and Iran's two-day Hormuz offer still stands
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday, November 21 that Iran is still open to talks with the US and that its offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in two days has not been withdrawn. He set firm conditions, so no deal is close.

beats.was: The US and Israel went to war with Iran on February 28. A framework deal in June broke down over shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, the sea lane for about a fifth of the world's oil, and the US now blockades Iran's ports. Qatar and Pakistan are carrying messages between the two sides.
beats.happened: Araghchi said Iran's plan still holds: the US lifts its recent sanctions on day one, and Iran reopens the strait and formal talks begin on day two. He said Washington's reply was unfavourable, that Iran wants signs the US is serious first, and that any deal must meet Iran's seven conditions, including keeping its enriched uranium at home. President Donald Trump said on Friday, November 20 that Iran wants a deal, but not one he can accept.
beats.means: Both sides say they want a deal but neither is moving, so the offer gives a path to reopening the strait without making it likely soon.
beats.fx: A small hint of a way out for the oil war premium, outweighed for now by the weekend's attacks.

impact.why: An open offer to reopen Hormuz points to lower oil if accepted, but the US has turned it down so far.
Japan buys most of its oil from the Gulf, so any real progress on Hormuz would ease pressure on the yen.

items.watch: Whether the US answers through Qatar or Pakistan, or lifts any sanctions, which would be the first step in Iran's plan.
